intro: A shadow, a quiet task, an imagined distant place and a revived historical style each change how close the viewer feels to the subject.
alt: Four studies show Microsoft in a dark scene, pouring at a window, viewing an imagined tiled interior and examining a fresco-like panel.

variants.name: Goya's art
variants.look: An isolated figure emerges from smoky darkness, with uneven marks and a narrow source of light.
variants.history: Francisco de Goya worked in Spain from the late eighteenth to the early nineteenth century. He moved among official portraits, prints, social critique and deeply unsettling late paintings.
variants.when: Study specific works for ways dark space and rough brushwork can make a scene psychologically tense.
variants.why: The eye searches the shadow for clues, leaving the subject's situation open to interpretation.

variants.name: Chardin's art
variants.look: A small domestic action happens in a softly lit room, with the mug, jug and figure arranged at a measured pace.
variants.history: Jean-Siméon Chardin painted still lifes and domestic scenes in eighteenth-century France.
variants.when: Study the space around hands and objects when a small, familiar action needs attention.
variants.why: Quiet color and restrained gestures make people notice the effort and texture of daily routine.

variants.name: Orientalism
variants.look: The pictured interior uses layered textiles and patterned tile to create an elaborate spectacle for the viewer.
variants.history: Numerous nineteenth-century European artists staged images of North Africa, the Middle East and Asia amid imperial unequal power. Their work ranges from observations to outright fantasy.
variants.when: Study the picture critically to see how stagecraft can turn a real place or tradition into an invented setting for others.
variants.why: Careful detail can make a fantasy seem authoritative. Comparing it with the people and places represented can expose the fabrication.

variants.name: Nazarenes
variants.look: Pale fields of color, deliberate outlines and restrained faces give the composition a painted-wall quality.
variants.history: Early nineteenth-century German-speaking artists in the Nazarene group sought a revival of Christian painting. They looked to Italian and German work from before the High Renaissance.
variants.when: Study the way a historical model can inform new outlines, colors and themes.
variants.why: Firm contours and a quiet order make gestures clearly readable even with little modeling.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Goya's art: brooding fictional scene with isolated modern woman, smoky deep-brown ground and rough asymmetric spotlight; Chardin genre painting: same woman pouring water into her mug beneath a quiet soft window with bare furnishings; Orientalism: modern woman visits a museum with a nineteenth-century European fantasy painting of opulent textiles and blue tile, emphasize painting is staged and artist's imagining rather than real cultural reportage, no stereotypes or pseudo-Arabic; Nazarenes: nineteenth-century revival pastiche with flat clear profile outlines, simple contemplative figures and measured fresco-like pale colors, modern visitor before study. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
